reports.title: Company PACs and the 2026 candidates
reports.html:
Descriptive patterns, not findings. Each link on the map says a company's own political action committee (PAC) gave to a candidate's campaign, backed by two facts: the PAC's FEC registration names the company as its sponsor, and the company is on the map by its SEC ID; the PAC's own FEC filings report the gifts. A PAC is funded by people who chose to give to it; it is influence, not control, and not the company's own treasury money.

Scope: 4,964 links from 258 companies' PACs to 507 candidates in the 2025-2026 cycle, $15,712,093 in all. Only companies the map can tie to their PAC by two facts are counted, not every corporate PAC. Candidate party, office and status are the FEC's own (candidate master file). FEC data through 2026-09-29.

reports.title: Company PACs: the committees that oversee them, and candidates who take none
reports.html:
Descriptive patterns from public FEC records and the House and Senate committee rosters, not findings. The records show who received money and who didn't, never why.

1. Do companies fund nearly everyone on their committees except a few?

No. Not one company funds two-thirds or more of the members who sit on the committees overseeing its industry and are on the 2026 ballot; the highest is Bristol Myers Squibb at about half. So a company 'skipping' a committee member is ordinary, not an exception.

Most of these are first-term members or newly appointed senators; smaller PACs (Aar Corp, Axon) give to fewer people overall.

4. Candidates who took $0 from corporate PACs this cycle

The FEC has no field for refusing PAC money. This list is the next best thing from its records: candidates in 2026-or-later races who raised $500,000 or more and received no money from corporate-sponsored PACs (FEC committee type C) in the 2025-2026 data. That is consistent with a no-corporate-PAC pledge, but not proof of one: a candidate may simply not have been given any, may have refunded gifts, or newer reports may not be in yet. 'Other PACs' is money from all other political committees (labor, ideological, leadership PACs). People the FEC lists under two candidate IDs (two races, or a re-registration, with the same money reported under each) are listed once, with both races.

324 candidates in all (320 on the 2026 ballot): challenger 186, open seat 121, incumbent 16, 1. Challengers and open-seat candidates often get little corporate PAC money anyway (it goes mostly to incumbents), so a $0 says the most for sitting members.
